submissions.findingTextShort: A 2026 plant-based IBS meta-analysis found pooled peppermint-oil symptom improvement, but many included studies were limited quality and larger trials remain needed.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2026 systematic review/meta-analysis of plant-based therapies for irritable bowel syndrome identified 60 eligible studies overall and pooled seven peppermint-oil studies. Peppermint oil favored placebo for dichotomous IBS symptom improvement with a pooled relative risk of 1.63 (95% CI 1.33 to 2.00). The authors also stated that the quality of many included studies was limited and called for further well-powered randomized trials. The review was published in 2026 but searched literature only through May 2024, so publication recency must not be treated as a post-2024 evidence window or as proof that later contradictory trials do not exist.
submissions.populationContext: Patients with IBS represented in seven pooled peppermint-oil studies within a broader plant-based therapy systematic review/meta-analysis.
submissions.usageContext: Oral peppermint-oil interventions for IBS; formulation differences remain relevant and pooled evidence cannot generalize to peppermint tea, aromatherapy, topical menthol, sweets, or fixed peppermint-plus-caraway products.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Limited study quality and the May 2024 search cutoff materially constrain certainty. Pooled positive evidence must remain visible together with direct null trials and formulation/population boundaries. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2026 multicenter pediatric randomized trial found peppermint-oil capsules were not superior to placebo for abdominal-pain treatment success or adequate relief in IBS/FAP-NOS.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2026 randomized controlled trial across 13 Dutch hospitals enrolled 228 children and adolescents aged 8 to 18 years with irritable bowel syndrome or functional abdominal pain-not otherwise specified. Peppermint-oil capsules were not superior to placebo for the primary endpoint of at least 30% abdominal-pain reduction after eight weeks, and adequate-relief rates were also not significantly different. Adverse events were mild and infrequent. This is direct population-specific null evidence and prevents adult/general pooled benefit signals from being represented as universal across pediatric IBS or functional abdominal pain.
submissions.populationContext: Children and adolescents aged 8 to 18 years with IBS or FAP-NOS across 13 Dutch hospitals.
submissions.usageContext: Oral peppermint-oil capsules under age-dependent protocol frequency with possible escalation for eight weeks; the trial regimen is research exposure, not consumer dosing guidance.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The null result applies to the pediatric IBS/FAP-NOS population and does not prove inefficacy in every adult population. Conversely, adult pooled benefit cannot override this direct pediatric evidence. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2022 meta-analysis of 10 RCTs / 1,030 IBS patients favored peppermint oil for global symptoms and abdominal pain, while adverse events were more frequent and overall evidence quality was very low.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2022 systematic review/meta-analysis of 10 randomized controlled trials involving 1,030 IBS patients found pooled benefit for global IBS symptoms and abdominal pain. Any adverse event was significantly more frequent with peppermint oil, and the authors rated the overall quality of evidence as very low. This finding therefore supports a positive pooled signal only when paired with low-certainty and adverse-event context and with individual rigorous null trials; it does not justify an unqualified efficacy statement or universal safety claim.
submissions.populationContext: One thousand thirty IBS patients across 10 randomized controlled trials included in the 2022 synthesis.
submissions.usageContext: Oral peppermint-oil RCTs with heterogeneous products and release characteristics; pooled research exposures are not generic consumer dosing guidance.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Very-low overall evidence quality and significantly higher adverse-event rates materially constrain certainty. Positive pooled estimates cannot erase direct null trials or reflux/tolerability context. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2021 Rome-IV adult randomized trial found enteric-coated peppermint oil did not significantly outperform placebo on IBS-SSS or secondary outcomes over six weeks.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2021 six-week randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial in adults with Rome-IV irritable bowel syndrome compared enteric-coated peppermint oil 180 mg three times daily with placebo. Both groups improved substantially from baseline, but the between-group difference in IBS Severity Scoring System change was not statistically significant and no secondary endpoint significantly favored peppermint oil. This rigorous null trial is first-class counterevidence to pooled positive efficacy estimates and directly contradicts a public summary that reports no disagreement.
submissions.populationContext: Adults with moderate-to-severe Rome-IV IBS at a single U.S. academic center.
submissions.usageContext: Enteric-coated peppermint oil 180 mg three times daily for six weeks; not equivalent to other release systems or non-oral preparations and not a consumer dosing recommendation.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The single-center design does not prove all peppermint-oil formulations are ineffective, but its null between-group results must remain visible alongside meta-analytic signals. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: The PERSUADE trial found neither small-intestinal- nor ileocolonic-release peppermint oil superior to placebo on regulatory co-primary IBS endpoints, despite selected secondary improvements with small-intestinal release.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: The PERSUADE double-blind trial randomized 190 Rome-IV IBS patients to 182 mg small-intestinal-release peppermint oil, 182 mg ileocolonic-release peppermint oil, or placebo for eight weeks, with 189 included in intention-to-treat analysis. Neither peppermint formulation significantly improved the FDA-style abdominal-pain response or EMA-style overall-relief co-primary endpoints versus placebo. Small-intestinal-release peppermint oil did improve selected secondary abdominal-pain, discomfort, and IBS-severity measures, while adverse events were mild but more common in both peppermint-oil groups. The trial is therefore mixed evidence with a strong formulation and endpoint boundary, not a simple positive or negative result.
submissions.populationContext: One hundred ninety adults with Rome-IV IBS randomized across four Dutch hospitals; 189 included in intention-to-treat analysis.
submissions.usageContext: Small-intestinal-release versus ileocolonic-release peppermint oil, each 182 mg for eight weeks. Release systems are distinct interventions and neither trial regimen is generic consumer dosing guidance.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Null regulatory co-primary endpoints must remain visible alongside positive secondary outcomes. Small-intestinal-release results cannot transfer to ileocolonic-release or arbitrary enteric products, and mild adverse-event excess remains part of the evidence balance. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.
